title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #5
description: Full-length 53-question simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes).

questions.prompt: A team wants to build a coding assistant that runs on their own infrastructure, needs built-in file read/write/edit and bash tools out of the box, and should support subagents and hooks without having to implement an agent loop from scratch. Which approach fits best?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which packages the Claude Code harness (built-in tools, agent loop, hooks, subagents) as a library that runs on infrastructure they control.

Managed Agents, since it is the only option that supports subagents and multi-agent coordination, and it conveniently also hosts the entire deployment and sandbox on Anthropic's infrastructure for them.
The Messages API Tool Runner, since it provides built-in file, edit, and bash tools automatically and only requires wiring up the request-execute loop for whatever custom tools the team wants to add.
A hand-written manual tool-use loop calling the Messages API directly, since hooks and subagent coordination can only be implemented by controlling every step of the loop yourself in custom code.

questions.explanation: The Claude Agent SDK is exactly this: a batteries-included harness (built-in tools, the agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions) that you host yourself. Managed Agents also supports multi-agent coordination but additionally hosts the deployment, which the team wants to control themselves, so option 2 is wrong. The Tool Runner only loops over tools you define and has no built-in file/bash tools, ruling out option 3. Hooks are a first-class Agent SDK feature, so a hand-rolled loop is not required, ruling out option 4.

questions.prompt: Your application parses Claude's reply as JSON, and about one run in fifty crashes on malformed output. What is the sturdiest fix?

options.text: Add "always return valid JSON" in capital letters to the prompt
Wrap the parse in a try block and silently skip failures
Lower the temperature to zero
Enforce the shape through tool use with a JSON schema, validate the result, and on validation failure retry with the error fed back

questions.explanation: Schema-enforced output plus a validation-retry loop treats model output as untrusted input and gives the model the information to correct itself. Louder instructions (A) reduce but do not eliminate failures, silent skipping (B) hides data loss, and temperature (C) does not guarantee syntax.

questions.prompt: Which change makes a repeated 10,000-token system prompt cheaper and faster without losing content?

options.text: Moving the prompt to the end of the request
Compressing the prompt text with abbreviations
Placing the stable prompt first and enabling prompt caching so the prefix is reused
Sending the prompt only on the first request of a session

questions.explanation: Caching reuses a stable prefix, cutting time-to-first-token and per-request cost. Position matters: stable content first

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest reason to put a queue between an application and the model?

options.text: It makes responses more accurate
It absorbs bursts so load stays within rate limits without dropping work
It reduces the token count
It removes the need for retries

questions.explanation: A queue smooths demand against a rate-limited dependency. It does not change accuracy (A) or token counts (C), and retries remain necessary (D)

questions.prompt: Token spend in production doubles in an hour. Many responses show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. Which SDLC hat are you wearing, and what is first?

options.text: Develop — invent a new agent framework
Operate — inspect logs, `request_id`, and the `max_tokens` cap before rewriting prompts
Maintain — float the model alias to latest
Implement — add more plugins

questions.explanation: This is operate/debug. Truncation is often `max_tokens`. Floating the alias makes it worse.

questions.prompt: `output_config.effort` is:

options.text: Another name for model tier
A separate thoroughness dial (thinking / tool density) from which model you picked
Required to enable streaming
Only valid with `temperature`

questions.explanation: Effort is independent of which model ID you chose. Not tied to temperature or streaming.

questions.prompt: API keys must not be stored in:

options.text: A secrets manager
Environment variables
The system prompt or chat history
A vault with egress substitution

questions.explanation: Prompts and history leak into logs and compaction.

questions.prompt: Production uses `model: "latest-sonnet"`. Quality shifts after an upstream release. Nobody changed application code. What should the team have done?

options.text: Deleted `CLAUDE.md`
Pinned an exact model ID and rerun evals before any upgrade
Raised `max_tokens`
Switched to WebSockets

questions.explanation: "Latest" is not a pin. Evals gate the next ID. Deleting `CLAUDE.md` and raising `max_tokens` do not freeze the model. Claude Messages does not use WebSockets.

questions.prompt: A hospital group is specifying an agent that drafts visit summaries under a HIPAA BAA. Which of the following is a valid **functional** requirement?

options.text: All processing must occur on infrastructure covered by the organization's BAA.
A clinician approves each draft summary before it enters the patient record.
The system must run on the hospital's approved cloud provider.
The agent should be fast and accurate.

questions.explanation: A functional requirement is checkable and describes the business process: a clinician approves each draft before it enters the record. BAA coverage and approved-cloud constraints are infrastructure requirements; "fast and accurate" is not checkable.

questions.prompt: A server streams Claude responses to mobile clients and appends the assistant turn to conversation history whenever its read loop ends. After a network drop mid-stream, a half-built `tool_use` block enters history and the next request fails validation. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Gate the history append on the `message_stop` event, discard the partial turn when a stream is interrupted, and retry from the last complete turn.
Append a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` after the partial block so the model knows the call failed.
Wrap the follow-up request in exponential backoff until the API accepts the turn.
Repair the partial JSON before appending, closing any unclosed braces.

questions.explanation: A read loop ending is not a message completing; only `message_stop` means the turn is whole. Gate the append on it, discard partials on interruption, retry from the last complete turn. Hand-repairing JSON or backoff cannot make a half-built turn valid.

questions.prompt: A security team must guarantee that no developer in the organization can allow Claude Code to edit environment files — even a developer who sets a bypass mode or adds an allow rule in project settings. Which control provides the most durable guarantee?

options.text: A defaultMode of "plan" set in each project's `.claude/settings.json`
A deny rule in enterprise `managed-settings.json`, which users and project files cannot override and which applies even when a bypass mode is set
An allow rule at the user level in `~/.claude/settings.json` scoped to safe paths only
A convention in each repository's CLAUDE.md stating that environment files must not be edited

questions.explanation: An enterprise-level deny rule in managed-settings.json is the most durable governance control: it cannot be removed by any individual developer, deny always wins over allow, and it applies even when a bypass mode is set. CLAUDE.md is a convention the model may not follow, and user/project settings can be overridden.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to contribute a full customer-service application — including its UI and deployment scripts — to the Claude Cookbook. What should the developer do for the contribution to be accepted?

options.text: Submit the whole application with extra documentation explaining each component
Strip out the reusable pattern and contribute it as a focused, self-contained example, because the Cookbook reviews one focused pattern rather than an entire application
Split the application into several simultaneous pull requests, one per component
Submit the application to the Cookbook but mark it as a draft so reviewers can take their time

questions.explanation: The Cookbook is built to review one focused, self-contained pattern, not an entire application; a whole application stalls regardless of code quality. Only the extracted reusable pattern goes to the Cookbook as a focused example.

questions.prompt: A customer on AWS assumes that every way of running Claude "on AWS" keeps inference inside their AWS boundary. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both Claude Platform on AWS and Claude in Amazon Bedrock run inference entirely inside the customer's AWS boundary
Claude in Amazon Bedrock routes inference to Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside AWS
Neither offering touches the customer's AWS account; both are Anthropic-hosted

Claude Platform on AWS is accessed through the customer's AWS account but inference is Anthropic-operated outside the AWS boundary, while Claude in Amazon Bedrock keeps data inside the customer's configured AWS boundary

questions.explanation: Claude Platform on AWS is accessed through the customer's AWS account using Anthropic's model IDs and lifecycle, but inference is Anthropic-operated outside the AWS boundary; Claude in Amazon Bedrock keeps data inside the customer's configured AWS boundary.

questions.prompt: While integrating a returns-processing assistant, an e-commerce platform's backend team sees a request fail with HTTP 429 and a rate-limit error. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Treat it as a permanent failure and stop calling the API for this feature entirely.
Back off and retry after a delay (ideally with exponential backoff and jitter), respecting any provided retry guidance.
Immediately retry the exact same request in a tight loop as fast as possible.
Silently swallow the error and return an empty response to the user.

questions.explanation: A 429 indicates a rate limit was hit — the correct response is backing off (typically exponential backoff with jitter) and retrying, not hammering the API or giving up permanently.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team wants application logic in a loan-underwriting assistant to branch correctly depending on why generation ended — for example, executing a tool when Claude requests one versus simply displaying the final answer. Which field should the application inspect?

options.text: The response's stop_reason field, which distinguishes cases like end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, and stop_sequence.
The length of the response text, inferring intent from character count.
The current system time, to guess whether a tool call is likely.
The HTTP status code alone, which is always 200 regardless of how generation ended.

questions.explanation: stop_reason tells the application why generation stopped (e.g., tool_use vs end_turn vs max_tokens), and is the correct signal for branching application logic — not status code, text length, or guesswork.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team needs a returns-processing assistant to stop generating cleanly at a specific delimiter the application relies on for parsing, rather than truncating mid-thought. What feature addresses this?

options.text: Reducing max_tokens until the delimiter happens to land at the cutoff.
Increasing temperature so Claude naturally stops earlier.
stop_sequences, which end generation as soon as a specified string is produced.
Removing the system prompt so output is shorter.

questions.explanation: stop_sequences let the application specify exact strings that, once generated, cleanly end the response — the right tool for a reliable, application-defined stopping point.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team wants Claude to analyze a scanned pay stub alongside a short text instruction in a single request for a loan-underwriting assistant. What is the correct way to structure this request?

options.text: Images cannot be combined with text in a single Claude request.
Include both an image content block and a text content block in the same message.
Send the image as a separate, unrelated API call and merge the two responses in application code.
Convert the image to a text description manually before calling the API at all.

questions.explanation: Claude's vision capability lets a single message include both image and text content blocks together, so the model reasons over both in one call.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants a returns-processing assistant to always adopt the same role, tone, and standing behavioral rules on every single call, regardless of what the end user types. Where should this persistent guidance live?

options.text: Nowhere — persistent behavior isn't configurable through the API.
Repeated at the end of every user message, worded slightly differently each time.
In the system prompt, which is the dedicated place for persistent, call-spanning instructions.
In a code comment in the backend service, unread by the model.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the dedicated parameter for persistent, standing instructions that should apply across every turn, separate from the specific user request.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how the "operate and maintain" phase of the systems life cycle applies specifically to a production Claude-powered application, as distinct from the initial development phase?

options.text: It primarily involves gathering the original business requirements, selecting the initial model version, and writing the first system prompt, tasks that are completed once during the initial build phase before the application goes live.

It involves ongoing tasks such as monitoring for model deprecation notices, tracking cost and latency trends, updating prompts as usage patterns drift, and re-validating behavior after any model version change.
It is considered complete as soon as the application passes initial user acceptance testing, after which the team can safely stop monitoring it unless a full system rebuild is later planned.

It only applies to traditional on-premises software deployments where a team controls the underlying servers, and has no meaningful relevance to API-based LLM integrations that are hosted by the provider.

questions.explanation: Operate-and-maintain is an ongoing phase covering monitoring, drift detection, and re-validation after changes such as model deprecations or version upgrades. Option A describes the requirements/design phase. Option C is wrong because production LLM applications require continuous attention, notably due to model deprecations and usage drift. Option D is factually incorrect; API-based systems still require ongoing operations.

questions.prompt: An internal coding agent's single system prompt has grown to include instructions for code review, documentation generation, test writing, and deployment troubleshooting, all crammed into one very long prompt. The team notices the agent frequently confuses which task it's supposed to perform, and response quality has degraded. Which refactoring approach best addresses this?

options.text: Add more CRITICAL/MUST-style emphasis and capitalized warnings to each section of the existing single monolithic prompt, so the model is forced to pay closer attention to every instruction simultaneously.

Split the monolithic prompt into separate, focused agents or skills for each distinct task (code review, documentation, testing, deployment), each with a scoped system prompt and only the tools relevant to that task, and route requests to the appropriate one.

Increase max_tokens substantially on every request so the model has more output room to work through the entire long, multi-task prompt before committing to a final response for whichever task was actually requested.

Leave the single monolithic prompt exactly as-is and wait for the model to improve, since Claude's large context window means raw prompt length has no measurable effect on task focus or instruction-following quality.

questions.explanation: This is a classic large-scale refactor: decomposing an overloaded monolith into focused, single-responsibility units with scoped context, mirroring good software design principles applied to prompts and agents. Adding more emphasis (A) doesn't fix the root cause and risks overtriggering. Increasing max_tokens (C) addresses output length, not task confusion caused by an unfocused prompt. Option D is contradicted by well-documented behavior; overloaded prompts degrade quality regardless of context window size.

questions.prompt: A production application currently pins its Claude API calls to a specific model ID rather than using a generic "latest" alias, and stores each system prompt revision with a version number alongside the model ID it was tuned for. What is the primary configuration-management benefit of this approach?

options.text: It guarantees the lowest possible per-token price available on the API, since pinning to a specific model ID locks in that model's pricing tier and shields the application from any future price increases Anthropic might apply to newer model versions.

It ensures behavior stays reproducible and stable until the team deliberately chooses to upgrade, and lets them track which prompt version was validated against which model version, avoiding silent behavior drift when Anthropic releases new models.

It is required because the Claude API rejects any request that omits an exact, dated, versioned model ID, meaning pinning is not really a deliberate design choice but a mandatory constraint every application must satisfy just to get a successful response.

It removes the need for any testing when a new model is eventually adopted, since a pinned model ID and versioned prompt automatically negotiate compatibility with the new model version and migrate the application's behavior without engineering involvement.

questions.explanation: Pinning model versions and tracking prompt versions against them gives reproducibility and traceability, preventing silent behavior drift from unannounced model changes. Option A is false; pinning has no inherent relationship to achieving the lowest price. Option C is false; model aliases are supported and requests are not rejected for using them. Option D is false; adopting a new model version still requires testing and validation.

questions.prompt: A task requires the model to plan across many interacting constraints and revise as it goes. What does this argue for?

options.text: The smallest model, to keep cost down
Splitting the task across several small models
A more capable model, since the work is reasoning-heavy
A longer prompt with the same model

questions.explanation: Multi-step reasoning under interacting constraints is where capability differences show. A small model (A) and splitting (B) both fragment the reasoning, and prompt length (D) does not add capability

questions.prompt: For a simple, high-volume classification task with tight latency requirements, which model tier is the best starting point?

options.text: Opus
Fable
Haiku
Whichever is newest

questions.explanation: Haiku is the default for simple, hot, cheap paths. Newest is not a strategy.

questions.prompt: A developer on the newest Claude models builds a UI that should show users the model's reasoning, but responses contain no thinking content even on hard requests where the model clearly reasoned. Why?

options.text: Thinking content is omitted from responses by default on the newest models; the developer must request summarized display when it needs to be shown.
Thinking only appears when `budget_tokens` is set explicitly.
Thinking content is available over raw REST but stripped by the SDK.
The requests were too easy to trigger reasoning; harder prompts would surface it.

questions.explanation: On the newest models thinking content is omitted from responses by default; request summarized display when it must be shown. `budget_tokens` is deprecated, and the SDK doesn't strip anything.

questions.prompt: A developer must estimate whether a request will fit within the model's context window. Which TWO items count against that token budget? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The HTTP status code of the response.
Tool definitions and tool results included in the request.
The API key sent in the request header.
The full conversation history sent with the request.
The server region the request is routed to.

questions.explanation: The context window holds everything at once: system prompt, full conversation history, injected documents, tool definitions, tool results, and the model's output. Transport details like status codes, API keys, and regions are not part of the token budget.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team is building an internal review assistant for a returns-processing assistant that needs strong reasoning over long documents, interactive response times where possible, and a moderate budget — with a human always reviewing the final output. What is the most appropriate default model strategy?

options.text: Use the most capable, highest-cost tier for every single request regardless of complexity.
Skip model selection entirely and use whichever tier responds first.
Use the fastest, cheapest tier for every request to minimize cost.
Use the balanced mid-tier model as the default, and evaluate edge cases that may need more capability.

questions.explanation: A balanced mid-tier model is the typical default when a task needs meaningful reasoning quality but doesn't justify the cost/latency of the most capable tier on every call, especially with human review as a backstop.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team repeatedly sends the same large static reference material (like a 90-page loan agreement) as part of the prompt on every request to a loan-underwriting assistant, with only the final question changing. What optimization reduces repeated cost and latency for this pattern?

options.text: Switching to a lower-quality model to compensate for the extra tokens.
Increasing max_tokens on every call.
Sending the reference material as a separate, disconnected API call each time.
Prompt caching, which lets the shared, unchanging prefix be reused across calls instead of being fully reprocessed each time.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching is designed exactly for this pattern: a large, unchanging prefix (like a static reference document or system prompt) reused across many calls, cutting repeated processing cost and latency.

questions.prompt: A pipeline must always run the same four steps in order: fetch a document, extract fields, validate them, and file the record. A teammate proposes an autonomous agent with tools for all four steps. What is the better design and why?

options.text: A workflow that calls the model for extraction inside deterministic orchestration, because the path is known in advance and determinism is cheaper and more reliable
The agent, because agents are more capable than fixed code
The agent, because it can skip steps when it decides they are unnecessary
Two agents supervising each other

questions.explanation: When the sequence is fixed, orchestrate it in code and use the model where the model adds value. Autonomy buys nothing on a known path and adds nondeterminism (B), skipping validation is a defect rather than a feature (C), and supervision hierarchies (D) are for problems that need delegation, not four fixed steps.

questions.prompt: What should terminate an agent loop?

options.text: A fixed wall-clock timeout only
The model deciding it is finished
An explicit success condition, with a step ceiling as a backstop
Running out of context

questions.explanation: A defined success condition ends the loop correctly, and the ceiling bounds the failure case. A timeout alone (A) does not recognize success, the model's own judgment (B) is not a guarantee, and exhausting context (D) is a failure rather than a termination

questions.prompt: You want Claude Code's Read/Edit/Bash loop inside your own CI job on your machines. Which option fits?

options.text: CMA session with tools listed on `sessions.create`
Claude Agent SDK `query()` (or `claude -p`) hosted by you
LangGraph, because only graphs can edit files
A single `messages.create` with no tools

questions.explanation: Agent SDK / headless Claude Code is the coding harness you host. CMA config does not live on the session. LangGraph is a general framework, not the only way to edit files. A tool-less Messages call cannot use Bash.

questions.prompt: A healthcare team is choosing a wiring path for an agent that processes Protected Health Information under a HIPAA BAA. Claude Managed Agents fits the workload operationally. What should the team do?

options.text: Use Managed Agents, since Anthropic's managed sandbox satisfies HIPAA requirements automatically
Use Managed Agents but disable session storage in the agent definition
Rule out Managed Agents — its sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so they are not currently eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA — and use the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration
Use Managed Agents in development and switch to a covered path only if an audit flags it

questions.explanation: Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, which is why they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA. The governing constraint picks the path: route PHI workloads to the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team is running a long-lived agent for a returns-processing assistant that needs to recall decisions and progress from earlier sessions, not just the current conversation. What capability addresses this?

options.text: Increasing temperature so the agent 'remembers' more creatively.
A larger max_tokens setting for the current request only.
Agent memory, which persists relevant state or context across sessions rather than starting from a blank slate each time.
Ignoring the need, since agents cannot retain any information across sessions.

questions.explanation: Agent memory is the mechanism for persisting relevant state or prior context across sessions, distinct from the current conversation's context window.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team is concerned an autonomous agent loop in a clinical intake assistant could keep taking actions indefinitely if it never reaches a satisfying stopping condition. What is the appropriate safeguard?

options.text: Rely solely on the end user to notice and manually kill the process every time.
Build in guardrails such as a maximum iteration count or checkpoints, so a runaway loop is bounded rather than open-ended.
No safeguard is needed, since agent loops always terminate on their own.
Remove all stopping logic so the agent can run as long as it likes.

questions.explanation: Bounding an agent loop with guardrails like a maximum iteration count or defined checkpoints is the correct safeguard against runaway or infinite-loop behavior.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team is automating patient intake forms processing for a clinical intake assistant: every case follows the same fixed sequence (extract fields, check policy rules, route exceptions to a human queue, generate a summary), and success is easy to verify. Which architecture is the best fit?

options.text: A fully autonomous agent that decides each next action for every case.
A deterministic workflow that calls Claude only at defined steps in a known sequence.
A long-running agent that must retain memory of every case indefinitely.
A manager agent that delegates every single case to specialized subagents.

questions.explanation: When the sequence and branching are known and fixed and success is easy to verify, a deterministic workflow is the better fit — an open-ended agent would add unnecessary variability the task doesn't need.

questions.prompt: A team wants an agent over their own custom tools, without hand-writing the request-execute-loop cycle, running on infrastructure they control. Which surface fits?

options.text: A hand-written loop over the messages endpoint, the only surface that will accept custom tool definitions.
The tool runner inside the regular SDK, which drives the loop over tools the team defines and hosts themselves.
The Claude Agent SDK, which supplies a loop plus built-in file, shell and search tools they have no use for.
Managed agents, which supply both the loop and a provider-hosted sandbox that this team would then have to run locally.

questions.explanation: Two questions separate these surfaces: who supplies the harness, and who supplies the deployment. The tool runner supplies the harness for tools you define while you keep hosting — exactly the stated requirements. The Agent SDK is the coding-agent harness with built-in tools, managed agents move hosting to the provider, and every surface accepts custom tools.

questions.prompt: Which change most improves reliability when a prompt must follow several constraints at once?

options.text: Adding emphasis to the most important constraint
Repeating the constraints at the end of the prompt
Raising the temperature so the model explores more options
Giving the model an example of a compliant output

questions.explanation: A worked example makes the constraints concrete and demonstrates their interaction, which prose cannot. Emphasis (A) and repetition (B) restate without clarifying, and higher temperature (C) increases variance, which is the opposite of reliability.

questions.prompt: Prompt cache *reads* are billed at roughly:

options.text: 2× input
1.25× input
~0.1× input
Free

questions.explanation: Reads ~0.1×. 1.25× / 2× are write premiums.

questions.prompt: To reduce context growth in a long tool-use session with extended thinking, a developer starts replacing older thinking blocks in history with short summaries before each request. The API begins rejecting the requests. Why, and what is the correct approach?

options.text: Summaries must be marked with a `summary: true` flag before resubmission.

Each thinking block carries a signature verifying it was not modified; blocks must be returned unchanged, and context pressure should instead be managed with context engineering (pruning tool results, compaction).
Only redacted thinking blocks may be summarized; the developer summarized normal blocks too.
Thinking blocks may be removed but never shortened; deleting them outright would have worked.

questions.explanation: Thinking blocks carry a signature verifying they were not modified; summarizing or editing them breaks it and the API rejects the request. Return blocks unchanged and manage context pressure with context engineering instead.

questions.prompt: A team must classify 50,000 support tickets into three labels in an overnight run and is deciding whether to enable extended thinking. What is the correct call?

options.text: Enable it at high effort so every classification is maximally accurate
Enable it with a small budget_tokens value to cap the reasoning cost per ticket
Leave it off — a one-word label needs no reasoning pass, and thinking tokens would multiply output cost across 50,000 calls with no accuracy gain
Enable it only for the first 1,000 tickets to calibrate the effort setting

questions.explanation: A one-word label needs no reasoning pass; enabling thinking multiplies output-token cost across 50,000 calls with no accuracy gain. A bare prompt with an output constraint is the right tool (and budget_tokens is deprecated, returning a 400 on the newest models).

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team is writing a long, complex prompt for a loan-underwriting assistant that mixes reference material, instructions, and an example together as one undifferentiated block of text, and Claude sometimes conflates the parts. What change most directly improves reliability?

options.text: Repeat the entire prompt twice in a row.
Remove all structure and make the prompt even shorter and vaguer.
Increase temperature so Claude interprets the ambiguity more creatively.
Wrap each distinct part (e.g., the document, the instructions, the example) in clear XML tags to delimit them.

questions.explanation: Using XML tags to clearly delimit distinct sections of a prompt (document, instructions, examples) is a documented best practice that reduces the model conflating unrelated parts.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team wants a clinical intake assistant to consistently adopt a specific persona and follow standing behavioral rules on every call, separate from whatever the user happens to type. Where does this belong?

options.text: Nowhere in particular — persona and standing rules cannot be set via prompting.
In the system prompt, since it's the dedicated place for persistent, call-spanning instructions.
In a separate, disconnected request sent before the real one.
Repeated inside every user message in slightly different wording.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the right home for persistent role and behavioral rules that should apply on every call, distinct from the specific per-turn user request.

questions.prompt: A developer is deciding whether to use Anthropic's official Python SDK or to hand-roll HTTP requests with a generic library like `requests` to call the Claude API. Which statement about the relationship between the SDK and the underlying REST API is accurate?

options.text: The official SDKs are a distinct product layered on top of a separate backend from the REST API, so requests issued through an SDK are metered against a different rate-limit pool and quota than requests made with raw HTTP calls.

The official SDKs are thin wrappers around the same REST API endpoints — adding conveniences like typed objects, automatic retries, and streaming helpers — but do not expose capabilities unavailable via raw HTTP.

Using an official SDK requires provisioning a dedicated SDK-specific API key that is distinct from the key used for raw HTTP requests, since the SDK authenticates through a separate credential system tied to the client library.

The SDK bypasses the need for authentication headers on each request because it establishes a persistent, server-side authenticated session with Anthropic on the client's behalf, similar to how some OAuth-based SDKs manage login state.

questions.explanation: The SDKs call the same REST endpoints under the hood and add developer conveniences (typed request/response objects, retries, streaming helpers) without unlocking hidden capabilities. Options A and C invent separate infrastructure that doesn't exist, and option D is wrong because the SDK still sends the same authentication headers on every request, just constructed for you.

questions.prompt: Three internal applications each need to query the same inventory service through Claude. The capability must be maintained by the platform team independently of the apps. What fits?

options.text: Each app embeds its own inventory tool with copied code
An MCP server exposing the inventory operations as tools, which all three applications connect to
Paste current inventory data into each app's system prompt daily
A Skill file describing the inventory API

questions.explanation: Reusable, independently maintained, model-facing capabilities are the MCP server's exact job. Copied tools (A) drift apart, pasted data (C) is stale and wastes context, and a Skill (D) carries instructions, not a live connection.

questions.prompt: On current Claude models, "CRITICAL: YOU MUST CALL THE TOOL" usually:

options.text: Reliably fixes under-triggering
Tends to over-trigger; prefer plain precise instructions
Is required by the API
Disables caching

questions.explanation: Over-trigger, not a reliable under-trigger fix.

questions.prompt: You have 80 overlapping tools. Context is huge and pick accuracy is falling. What is the right tool-search setup?

options.text: Set `defer_loading: true` on the search tool to save tokens
Keep the search tool loaded, defer cold tools, still send every schema in `tools`
Omit deferred schemas from `tools` so the body stays small
Merge all 80 tools into one mega-tool with a `mode` enum

questions.explanation: Never defer the search tool. The server still needs full schemas to search and expand `tool_reference`. A mega-tool hides the same ambiguity in a parameter.

questions.prompt: A team connects several MCP servers through the API MCP Connector and notices a large amount of the context window is consumed by tool definitions before the first message arrives. What is the module-recommended way to control this cost?

options.text: Nothing is needed — MCP tool definitions only enter the context window when a tool is actually called
Configure mcp_toolset with defer_loading and enabled settings (with the required mcp-client beta header) to defer definitions and expose only the tools the model should see
Switch all servers to the stdio transport, which does not load definitions into context
Increase max_tokens so the model has room for both the definitions and its response

questions.explanation: MCP servers add tool definitions to context even when unused. The mcp_toolset's defer_loading delays loading a definition until needed and enabled exposes only chosen tools; both require the mcp-client-2025-11-20 beta header. The Connector also only supports remote HTTP servers, not stdio.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team always wants a clinical intake assistant to call a specific tool — never answer directly — whenever a user asks about order or account status. What controls this behavior?

options.text: The max_tokens parameter, which limits response length only.
There is no way to require a specific tool call — Claude always decides freely.
The tool_choice parameter, which can force Claude to use a specific tool rather than deciding on its own.
The temperature parameter, which has no relationship to tool selection.

questions.explanation: tool_choice lets the application force Claude to use a specific named tool (or any tool, or none), rather than leaving the decision entirely to the model.

questions.prompt: A team's prompt instructs Claude to classify support tickets into one of five categories and return just the category name. Despite clear written instructions, outputs vary: sometimes a full sentence, sometimes the category plus an explanation, sometimes different capitalization. What change is most likely to produce consistent, correctly formatted output?

options.text: Add three or four few-shot examples to the prompt, each pairing a sample support ticket with the exact category-only output format desired, so the model has concrete patterns to imitate.

Rewrite the same classification instruction in all capital letters throughout the prompt, on the assumption that visual emphasis like all-caps text makes the model adhere more strictly to the required format.
Set max_tokens to 1 on every request so the response is hard-truncated at a single token, ensuring the model cannot append any explanation after the category name.
Remove the explicit list of five categories from the prompt, giving the model more open-ended flexibility to decide on its own which label best fits each ticket.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that demonstrate the exact input/output pattern are one of the most reliable ways to lock in a consistent output format, often more effective than instructions alone. Capitalizing text for emphasis has little reliable effect on model behavior. Setting max_tokens=1 would truncate output mid-token for most category names, breaking it rather than fixing it. Removing the category list would make the classification task ambiguous, not more consistent.

questions.prompt: Content retrieved from an external site contains instructions aimed at the model. What is the correct defense?

options.text: Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore such content
Treat retrieved content as untrusted data and bound the model's permissions outside the prompt
Scan for known injection phrases and block them
Use a model with a larger context window

questions.explanation: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its granted permissions regardless of what the content says. Prompt instructions (A) and phrase filters (C) are bypassable, and context size (D) is irrelevant

questions.prompt: Assemble the minimal secure configuration for an agent that fetches untrusted web content and writes results to a single protected path under a scoped identity. Which TWO pieces belong? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A system-prompt line telling the model to ignore instructions in fetched pages, relied on as the enforcement layer.
A PreToolUse hook that runs before `write_file`, denies any write outside `/workspace/output`, and logs the attempt.
A retry wrapper with exponential backoff around the write call.
The API key drawn from an environment variable or secret manager rather than committed configuration.
Broad filesystem access for the agent, balanced by a weekly review of the audit log.

questions.explanation: The PreToolUse hook is the enforcement layer (deny out-of-bounds writes before execution, and log), and secrets come from the environment or a secret manager, never committed config. A prompt line is not enforcement, a retry wrapper is error handling, and broad access with weekly log review violates least privilege.

questions.prompt: A user of a loan-underwriting assistant tries to get Claude to ignore its safety guidelines by framing the request as a fictional roleplay scenario. What is the correct posture for the application to take?

options.text: Assume jailbreak attempts are not a real concern once a system prompt exists.
Disable logging so the attempted jailbreak isn't recorded.
Treat the fictional framing as a legitimate exception and relax safety guardrails for the roleplay.
Maintain the same safety guardrails regardless of framing, and add application-level checks rather than relying on the model's judgment alone.

questions.explanation: Jailbreak attempts often use reframing (roleplay, hypotheticals) to bypass guidelines — the correct posture keeps guardrails consistent regardless of framing, backed by application-level checks rather than the model alone.

questions.prompt: A DevOps team gives a Claude Code agent shell access to help automate routine infrastructure tasks. They are concerned the agent could be prompted, accidentally or via injected content, into running destructive commands like rm -rf on shared paths or a forced push to the production branch. Which control most directly prevents the destructive command from ever executing?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt asking the agent to exercise caution around destructive commands like rm -rf or a forced push, relying on the model's own judgment to decline unsafe requests.
Configure a PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash tool calls against a deny-list of destructive command patterns and blocks matching calls before they run.
Configure a PostToolUse hook that captures the exact Bash command and its resulting output, writing them to a log immediately after the command has already finished executing.
Increase the model's context window size, on the theory that a longer retained history helps it remember not to run destructive commands like rm -rf or a forced push.

questions.explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs before tool execution and can deny the call outright, making it the only option here that stops a destructive command from executing at all. A system-prompt request (option A) is advisory and unenforced, a PostToolUse hook (option C) only observes after the command has already run, and context window size (option D) has no bearing on enforcing a safety control.

questions.prompt: A team is building an MCP server for their project-management tool. They want Claude to be able to read open ticket data as context, and separately want to give users a reusable, parameterized workflow template for triaging tickets that doesn't require any specific action to be performed. Which combination of MCP primitives best fits these two needs?

options.text: Expose both the ticket data and the triage workflow as MCP Tools, treating Tools as the only primitive worth implementing since they are the most commonly supported primitive across MCP clients and Claude applications.
Expose the ticket data as MCP Resources for Claude to read as context, and the triage workflow as an MCP Prompt that can be invoked as a reusable template
Expose the ticket data as an MCP Prompt so it can be templated for Claude, and expose the reusable triage workflow as an MCP Resource that the application reads directly as context.
Combine everything into a single MCP Resource with a query parameter that dynamically returns either raw ticket data or triage workflow instructions depending on how the client calls it.

questions.explanation: Resources are the right primitive for exposing readable context like ticket data without invoking an action, and Prompts are the right primitive for a reusable, parameterized workflow template — Tools are best reserved for actions that perform operations. Treating Tools as the only usable primitive misuses them for passive data access. Swapping Prompts and Resources inverts their purposes: Prompts are templates, not raw data, and Resources are data, not workflow templates. Combining everything into one Resource that branches on a query parameter blurs the Resource/Tool distinction instead of using the primitives as designed.
